name: MARPE (mini-implant palate expander)

lead: MARPE widens a narrow upper jaw in late adolescents and adults without surgery. It looks like a conventional expander but is fixed to the roof of the mouth with small bone screws, so the force splits the palate rather than just tipping the teeth.

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed for cheekbone width, midface support and breathing. A 2021 meta-analysis and CBCT studies report skeletal expansion along with some dental change in late adolescents and young adults. Published research covers bite and skeletal change; a trial of 3D facial soft tissue change and perceived appearance is registered.

paras: An orthodontist fits the appliance with two to four mini-implants and the expander screw is turned gradually over weeks, then held for months, usually followed by braces. Users on forums report costs in the thousands of dollars.

Reported issues include incomplete suture opening in some patients, tooth tipping, pain, soreness, screw loosening or failure, and expansion greater at the front of the palate than the back. It is a prescription orthodontic procedure; long-term stability and facial appearance studies are limited.

angle.text: Teens and young adults use MARPE to widen the upper jaw without cutting bone, and forum users hope for a broader midface and cheekbone support. Studies show skeletal widening for narrow jaws; cosmetic facial effects are barely studied.

lead: MARPE (micro-implant or miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion) is an orthodontic technique for widening the upper jaw in patients whose midpalatal suture is no longer easily opened by a conventional tooth-borne expander. The appliance is anchored to the palate with mini-implants and is used to treat maxillary transverse deficiency, a narrow upper jaw associated with crossbite, crowding and, in some patients, nasal airway restriction [1][2].

Clinical reports describe it as a non-surgical option for adults and late adolescents, as an alternative to surgically assisted expansion [1][2]. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis examined its efficacy in late adolescents and adults [3], and a randomized trial compared conventional expansion with MARPE using low-dose CBCT [4]. A named variant, the Maxillary Skeletal Expander (MSE), uses four bicortical mini-implants [5].

In looksmaxxing culture MARPE is discussed as a way to widen the maxilla and, proponents say, improve midface width and breathing [6][7]. The published literature addresses skeletal and dental outcomes; a trial of three-dimensional facial soft tissue changes and perceived appearance after MARPE is registered but not yet recruiting [8].

paras: A conventional rapid palatal expander is attached to the upper molars and works well in children, where the midpalatal suture is still open. In older patients, researchers note that expansion forces transmitted through the teeth can produce unwanted dental effects rather than true skeletal expansion, which prompted the development of mini-implant-supported designs [2][9].

In MARPE, mini-implants are placed in the palate and connected to the appliance, so that force is applied directly to bone. Finite element analyses have modelled how stress is distributed through the nasomaxillary complex with such appliances [10][11].

A case report describes a 19-year-old patient with maxillary constriction treated with a MARPE appliance and reports orthopedic correction of the deficiency [2]. A clinical article from 2017 describes non-surgical treatment of transverse deficiency in adults using MARPE [1].

Imaging studies of the MSE appliance in CBCT scans examined changes in the midpalatal and pterygopalatine sutures [5], and a CBCT study of young adults reported skeletal and dentoalveolar changes after miniscrew-assisted expansion [12]. A separate study examined the stability of these changes after treatment [13].

A prospective randomized clinical trial compared conventional rapid palatal expansion with MARPE using low-dose CBCT [4]. A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of MARPE in late adolescents and adults assessed its efficacy [3].

Registered trials include studies of MARPE with and without corticopuncture [14][15], of two versus four mini-screws in non-growing patients [16][17], of speech effects [18], of sleep and airway [19], and of three-dimensional facial soft tissue changes and perceived appearance [8].

The published evidence concerns correction of a narrow maxilla and the proportion of skeletal versus dental change. Reviewers describe a pursuit of 'pure orthopedic movement' as a goal that is approached but not always reached [9]. Patients' age and suture maturity are among the factors discussed in the literature [1][3].
No published trial in the sources reviewed here has established that MARPE changes facial attractiveness; the registered soft-tissue study [8] has not yet reported.

Users on looksmax.org discuss MARPE as a hardmaxx intervention, often in connection with palate width, cheekbone projection and breathing [6][7]. Some posters report their orthodontist's predicted expansion (for example about 6 mm for a teenager) and debate whether this is enough to justify the cost [7].

Threads also discuss whether widening could be unflattering for people who already have wide faces [20][21], how to obtain it, and combinations with facemask treatment or surgery [22][23][24]. These accounts are anecdotal.
